subject: Reserved node queueing & latency variance — proposal and questions from Aurora Energies
messages:
From: James Wallace <james.wallace@aurora-energies.com>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@aurora-energies.com, laura_bennett@redwood.com
Date: 2026-08-01T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Reserved nodes — latency variance & queueing for weekday peaks

Marcus —

Thanks for the demo last week. We're close to internal approval for a 48-GPU reserved pool with Redwood, but procurement and infra asked for a few clarifications before we lock the commit: 

- Aurora runs a predictable daily ramp 05:30–09:30 PDT where latency sensitivity is high. We need clarity on how reserved nodes are prioritized vs. burst workloads (other customers) during that window.
- Can Redwood guarantee a 95th-percentile token latency bound for requests served from the reserved pool? If not, what typical variance should we expect and under what conditions might that be breached?
- Queueing behavior: will requests be queued behind higher-priority dedicated traffic from other customers? We need deterministic behavior or a documented preemption policy.

I've attached a short demand profile (aurora_demand_profile.csv) showing our hourly token/seq mix; it highlights the weekday morning peak. Procurement also needs a short SLA appendix we can send to legal.

Can you loop in the right folks and propose language we can show legal by EOD Tuesday?

Thanks —
James Wallace
Director, Cloud Infrastructure
Aurora Energies

Attachments: aurora_demand_profile.csv (CSV, 12KB)

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: James Wallace <james.wallace@aurora-energies.com>
Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.com
Date: 2026-08-01T10:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Reserved nodes — latency variance & queueing for weekday peaks

James — thanks for the clear notes and the demand profile. I'm glad the demo was useful.

Quick answers up front:
- Reserved pools are logically isolated capacity with prioritized scheduling; by default your traffic is routed to your reserved nodes first.
- We can provide an operational SLA framed around availability (GPU pool uptime) and an empirical p95 token latency observation window, but an absolute hard cap on p95 latency across all request shapes is risky because of tail behaviors (very long context, sudden batch spikes).

I'll escalate to our Capacity & Runtime teams to translate the ask into specific numbers and an appendix you can hand to legal. Can you confirm: 1) exact daily peak window you need prioritized (is 05:30–09:30 PDT firm?), and 2) committed monthly GPU count (48 for now)?

Proposed near-term next steps:
- I will send a draft SLA appendix that proposes a prioritized queue for your reserved pool during the peak window and an operational definition for when burst preemption may occur.
- If acceptable, we'll include monitoring hooks and an alerting contract (token-level telemetry, webhook) for real-time visibility.

If you confirm the two items above I'll follow up with the draft by Monday.

—Marcus
Marcus Lin
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

Subject: Fwd: Reserved nodes — latency variance & queueing for weekday peaks (internal)

Folks — forwarding James' ask and Marcus' reply. TL;DR: Aurora wants deterministic priority on their reserved pool for a morning peak and an SLA appendix we can hand to legal.

Notes from capacity side (draft thinking):
- We can mark the 48-GPU pool as "priority-backed" so scheduler will favor Aurora's queued requests on that pool during their declared window. This makes reserved pool behavior deterministic for most traffic shapes.
- For very large batch/long-context requests we should call out that transient KV/cache misses and memory compaction can push p95 out; recommend an agreed operational threshold (e.g., p95 token latency <= 120ms for typical 1k token requests).
- Suggest a burst design: a small shared burst pool (up to 12 GPUs) that Aurora can consume when reserved pool is saturated. Consumption of the burst pool is preemptible under system pressure — we should state a preemption policy clearly (first-preempt, 5-minute notification window + graceful drain).

Action items for sales/legal appendix draft:
1) Commit to prioritized scheduling for 05:30–09:30 PDT (customer confirms).
2) Propose p95 observation: target <= 120ms for requests under 1k tokens; include a shiproom clause that defines capacity exhaustion events.
3) Define burst pool size and preemption rules.

I've sketched wording in redwood_sla_draft_v2.docx (internal). Marcus, if you want I can attach a cleaned version to send to James.

—Laura
Laura Bennett
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
laura_bennett@redwood.com

Attachments: redwood_sla_draft_v2.docx (internal draft)

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: James Wallace <james.wallace@aurora-energies.com>
Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.com, procurement@aurora-energies.com
Date: 2026-08-03T08:45:00-07:00
Subject: Revised SLA appendix and queue-priority proposal (draft)

James —

Thanks for confirming the 48-GPU commitment over the call yesterday. Attached is a draft SLA appendix (redwood_sla_draft_v2.docx) that captures the prioritized scheduling behavior and a proposed p95 observation target. Highlights: 

- Peak window: 05:30–09:30 PDT (customer-declared). Redwood will route Aurora traffic to the reserved 48-GPU pool first during this window.
- p95 token latency objective: target <= 120ms for requests with <= 1,000 tokens under normal operating conditions. This is an objective with an operational review clause for capacity events.
- Burst pool: up to 12 GPUs available on-demand; burst consumption is preemptible if the system enters a cross-customer emergency or capacity shortfall. Preemption policy: 5-minute warn, graceful drain (current requests allowed to finish), and automatic fallback to shared capacity routing if needed.
- Monitoring & alerts: we will emit token-level p95 metrics and an alert webhook to your SRE channel when the p95 exceeds the objective for two continuous 5-minute windows. We can add a scheduled daily report.

If this aligns with Aurora's needs I recommend: 1) you send this to legal with a note that the p95 line is an operational objective (not an absolute SLA cap) and 2) we iterate on exact language for preemption compensation (credits) if desired.

Attached: redwood_sla_draft_v2.docx (SLA appendix draft).

Next step: can we get a legal point of contact so we can prepare a redline-ready copy?

—Marcus

Date: 2026-08-03T15:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Revised SLA appendix and queue-priority proposal (draft)

Marcus — appreciate the quick turnaround and the clear appendix. A few items from procurement/legal side: 

- We can accept the p95 objective language but procurement wants to see a short credit schedule for sustained breaches (e.g., p95 > 120ms for more than 3 hours in a month). Could your legal ops team propose a simple credit ladder?
- For the burst pool: can you confirm whether burst GPU consumption will be meterable separately (we prefer line-item visibility on invoices)?
- Monitoring: please include the webhook endpoint example and a sample payload so our SREs can validate ingestion.

If you can provide those three items (credit ladder, burst metering commitment, webhook sample) we'll route this to our legal team for a redline. Happy to schedule a 30-min sync if that's easier.

Thanks —
James Wallace
Director, Cloud Infrastructure
Aurora Energies
